anchors.fact: In 1879 Stevenson crossed the Atlantic and then the continent to reach Fanny in California (Sanchez, *Life of Mrs. R. L. Stevenson*, 1920, ch. V; the *Amateur Emigrant* dedication is signed 1879). He sailed from Glasgow and touched at Greenock; no port in the reading. He didn't go steerage: he took the second cabin, which sat in the middle of the steerage decks, so he'd have a table to write at (*The Amateur Emigrant*, "The Second Cabin", Gutenberg #627).
anchors.meaning: Going towards someone, at a cost, with no way back.
anchors.speaksTo: story test 1–2; the one true thing (rebels towards someone)

anchors.fact: His parents objected at first: not to her divorce, but to his choosing an American and a stranger. Once they saw his mind was made up for good, they gave way completely, promised an allowance and got ready to welcome her (Sanchez ch. V). His father's help after the wedding was generous and freely given (Colvin, intro to the *Letters*, Gutenberg #31809).
anchors.meaning: The world bent to a mind made up. One clause in the middle, never the ending (*Asked In* owns being let in).

anchors.fact: They went quietly "across the bay" and married on 19 May 1880 (the city is not on the page), with two witnesses, and took Fanny's son Sam, about twelve, with them (Sanchez ch. V).
anchors.meaning: The start of the life, not the end of the chase.

anchors.fact: That summer four of them squatted in an abandoned miners' bunkhouse on Mount Saint Helena. He called himself and Fanny the King and Queen of Silverado, Sam the Crown Prince, and Chuchu the dog (a setter crossed with a spaniel) the Grand Duke. Their first act of taking the place was cutting out the poison oak growing inside (*The Silverado Squatters*, "The Act of Squatting", Gutenberg #516).
anchors.meaning: A stop made on their own ground, and they crowned themselves in it.
anchors.speaksTo: test 3; Wren's position (stop where you choose)

anchors.fact: Why the mountain: his health and their purse. Fanny was told nothing else would save his life, and they couldn't afford a resort (her 1883 letter, via Sanchez ch. V; also the fog, same chapter). "Rent-free, into a ready-made house" is what tempted him, said of the idea and of another place (Pine Flat) first.
anchors.meaning: The reading gives no reason for the mountain and never says they went up to be free.

anchors.fact: They kept their wine in the old mine tunnel (*Silverado*, "Episodes in the Story of a Mine"); Nellie says the tunnel's mouth was the one place that was always cool (Sanchez ch. V).
anchors.meaning: The cold, dark place the wine waits in: the drink's overnight step.

anchors.fact: At night one candle stood in the neck of a pint bottle, and, seen from outside on the platform where he walked, the cracked old house seemed to burst with light through its chinks; you'd have taken it for a fire. A traveller on the far hills, if one had been there, would have stopped to watch it (*Silverado*, the book's last paragraph).
anchors.meaning: A life that stopped still looked, from outside, like something burning. The watcher is an "if": never "people saw".

anchors.fact: In Schram's cellar, "the oldest vineyard in the valley" (eighteen years old, Stevenson guessed), he tasted everything, including a "Hock" and a Golden Chasselas, while Fanny sat on the veranda with Mrs Schram (*Silverado*, "Napa Wine").
anchors.meaning: The wine of the place they'd chosen, on his own page.

anchors.fact: Oxford traces the Highball back to white wine and soda water, the Austrian Spritzer (HIGHBALL, pdf 1005). **Owned link, one clause:** Schram's "Hock" was a Californian wine sold under the German style name, and "hock" is the word Oxford uses for German white wine. We never say Stevenson drank wine and soda, a Spritzer or a Highball. Byron stays out (hangover cure: medicine; and the Thrill Seeker's backup).
anchors.meaning: Our long glass descends from a drink made with the kind of wine he tasted.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; "let the drink sound worth having"

anchors.fact: At sunrise and late at night the scent of sweet bay filled the canyon (*Silverado*, "Toils and Pleasures"); bay also among the afternoon smells in "The Act of Squatting". The page doesn't say which tree; our kitchen bay leaf is a stand-in, never "his bay", and never a reason to pick a wild leaf.
anchors.meaning: The scent of the place, put in the bottle before the pour.
anchors.speaksTo: the spark (Wren rules on the *Just Knew* echo)

anchors.fact: The marriage gave them "fourteen rich years" together, Nellie wrote, counting from the wedding (Sanchez ch. V). In Samoa, she says, "home" first meant something to them: they bought land near Apia, named the place Vailima ("five waters", for its stream) and set about clearing the forest, with hired Samoan workers, and building the house (ch. VIII, printed p. 167). To the end it was their custom (Sanchez uses the phrase in ch. VII and ch. VIII) that he brought her each morning's writing for her verdict (ch. VIII).
anchors.meaning: It holds past the page: they stopped again, on ground they chose, and the love didn't cool.
anchors.speaksTo: test 4; the Lover's fear (love going cold) answered

anchors.fact: Stevenson put a line of Cicero over the book (*De Officiis* I.xx). In Walter Miller's translation (Loeb 1913), such people living quietly in the country have kings' aims, "to be subject to no authority, to enjoy their liberty, that is, in its essence, to live just as they please" (§70). Counterweight: Cicero goes straight on to rank public life higher (§70–71).
anchors.meaning: Stevenson's own framing of stopping as freedom, his choice of where to cut, not Cicero's verdict.

anchors.fact: A colder liquid holds more dissolved CO2 at the same pressure (*Liquid Intelligence*, printed p. 289).

cocktail.closingLine: Ice first, soda last. Then pour it where you mean to land, and unpack.
cocktail.glassware: a tall stemmed wine glass, filled with ice
method: The evening before, push one dried bay leaf into a bottle of dry California white, put the cork back in, and stand the bottle in the coldest, darkest corner of the fridge. The leaf stays in the bottle.
Put the soda water in the fridge too.
Fill a tall stemmed wine glass with ice.
Pour in 135 ml of the cold wine.
Top it with 45 ml of cold soda, poured gently so it keeps its bubbles, and give it one slow turn with a spoon.
cocktail.name: Rent-Free

recipe.item: dry California white wine (crisp and unoaked, a dry Riesling style), with a bay leaf left in the bottle overnight
recipe.note: he tasted one sold as "Hock" in a Napa cellar; kept cold in the dark, the way they kept theirs in the tunnel
goes into the wine bottle, and stays there

cocktail.tagline: You love like it's a getaway. Even where you stop is a hideout.

reading.epigraph: Its wine spends a night in the cold, as two newlyweds kept theirs: in a mine.
whoYouAre: A one-way ticket. A job left on a Friday. A family dinner where you finally told them, and the table went quiet. You've chosen people, places and whole lives like that: all at once, and usually against advice. And every time, choosing and getting free felt like the same thing. Whoever you fell for was also the way out.

You'd never tell anyone how much you'd like to land somewhere. It feels like giving in. Being parked is the real fear: someone else deciding where you stop, and the life you ran towards slowly picking up the rules of the one you ran from.
And whoever you choose never has to guess. They know they were picked over everything else. Next to you, love looks like courage, and anyone watching starts asking what they'd leave for theirs.
yours: In 1879 a young Scottish writer, Robert Louis Stevenson, crossed the Atlantic and then the whole of America to reach Fanny, an American, in California. The next spring, they married. His parents had objected, because she was "an American and a stranger", and when they saw his mind was made up, they gave in completely.

After the wedding, they moved into an abandoned miners' bunkhouse high on a mountain above the Napa Valley, with Fanny's son and their dog, and lived there as squatters. What had tempted him was the idea of going "rent-free, into a ready-made house". He crowned the two of them "the King and Queen of Silverado", and his first job, to take possession, was cutting out the poison oak that had grown up through the floor. They kept their wine in the old mine tunnel, the one place on that hot hillside that stayed cool.

His book about that summer ends at night, with a single candle stuck in the neck of a bottle. From outside, he wrote, the old cracked house seemed to burst with light, and anyone out on the far hills would have stopped to watch. I like to think that's what stopping looks like for you: not being caught, but choosing the place, and making it as wild as the road. Years later, in Samoa, they bought land, set about clearing it and building a house, and called the place Vailima. Fanny's sister wrote that it was there "home" first came to mean something to them, and he was still bringing her each morning's writing to judge.

The cocktail I've made for you is a wine highball: white wine and soda, one of the long, light drinks the highball is traced back to. In a Napa cellar he tasted a wine sold as "Hock", the English name for German white wine, so here it's a crisp, dry California white. The evening before, one bay leaf goes into the bottle, and the bottle goes into the coldest, darkest corner of the fridge, as a nod to the tunnel, and to a canyon he wrote smelled of sweet bay at sunrise and late at night. Then it's poured over ice into a tall stemmed wine glass, and topped with soda straight from the fridge.

When the pull to go comes again, ask yourself what you'd be leaving. If it's someone deciding for you, go. If it isn't, stop, on purpose, in a place of your choosing, and make that the adventure. Being caught means someone else chose where you'd end up. Stopping means you did.
